Intuit stock: TD Cowen lifts target to 350 dollars, keeps Hold
sum: TD Cowen raised its price target for Intuit Inc. from 346 to 350 US dollars on Monday, November 9, while keeping a Hold rating on the shares. The analyst cited valuation in the decision but maintained a neutral view on the near-term setup, according to Investing.com.

TD Cowen said the first-quarter outlook offered few expected catalysts. The firm also pointed to artificial intelligence risks and competitive intensity as continuing issues for the financial-management software company, which serves consumers, small businesses and accounting professionals through products including TurboTax, QuickBooks and Credit Karma.

The assessment leaves investors focused on whether Intuit can turn its AI investments into stronger customer engagement and operating efficiency. At the same time, competition remains a strategic challenge, particularly in tax software and adjacent financial services. The Hold rating signals an expectation that the shares will perform broadly in line with the market over the coming months rather than deliver a clear near-term outperformance.

TD Cowen identified Intuit's third-quarter earnings report as the next potential catalyst. The report is expected to provide preliminary insight into the fiscal 2027 tax season, making customer trends and management commentary important indicators for the company's growth profile. The analyst view therefore places greater weight on operating evidence than on the target-price increase alone.

sum: Intuit expanded its Intuit Intelligence platform on October 27, adding AI-powered workflows across QuickBooks, Intuit Enterprise Suite and Intuit Accountant Suite. The announcement came at Intuit Connect in Las Vegas, according to Intuit.
Intuit stock traded at 300.43 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 17:02 CET on Monday, November 9, 2026.

The company is positioning Intuit Intelligence as a unified platform that combines financial data, industry expertise, artificial intelligence and human oversight. Intuit says the system orchestrates more than 60 specialized language models and over 100 AI skill agents across more than 100 workflows and 74 financial domains.

For accounting firms, Agentic Books Close is designed to automate more of the monthly close process while following each firm's procedures and recording actions in an audit log. Accountants remain responsible for supervision, review, approvals and exceptions. Firm Playbooks and portfolio intelligence are in beta.

Intuit Enterprise Suite is adding industry-specific capabilities for construction, manufacturing and nonprofits. Manufacturing workflows cover multi-location inventory and production, while nonprofit customers are set to receive fund and grant accounting. Revenue Management capabilities based on the Sequence acquisition are also planned.

QuickBooks is adding AI-powered invoicing and cash-flow tools that identify aging invoices, compare performance with peers and automate customer follow-up. Intuit says these tools help businesses get paid four days faster on average, based on its comparison of customers using the AI features with customers using standard reminders.

The announced capabilities are rolling out to U.S. businesses and accounting firms, but availability differs by product. Agentic Books Close is in a pilot with selected customers, while several Enterprise Suite functions remain in beta or are scheduled for a later release. ProPartner, a training and certification program for accounting firms, is planned for early 2027.

Intuit stock broadens AI platform for accountants and businesses
sum: Intuit is broadening its AI platform for accountants and businesses as it seeks to automate more financial workflows and deepen customer engagement. In a post published on November 4, Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi described the company's strategy and outlined new capabilities presented at Intuit Connect, based on opening remarks from October 26.

Goodarzi said Intuit is building one unified platform for accounting firms and their clients. The system combines customer data, financial applications, domain expertise, and AI-enabled workflows, while leaving users in control of decisions and approvals. Intuit says the goal is to support both top-line growth and greater operating efficiency.

A central feature is Agentic Books Close, which is designed to follow a firm's own procedures for managing transactions and closing books. The agent tracks progress, flags items that require attention, and can prepare a financial summary for a client. Intuit said the feature is being tested in beta, with some capabilities available now and others expected to reach customers within three to six months.

Accountant Suite is also being expanded with Agent Studio, allowing firms to create, deploy, and monitor workflows for specific client needs. Intuit said it is building the tool with about 20 firms and that some participants already have agents running. Another planned capability, Advisory Insights, is intended to identify unusual expenses, falling profits, and potential investment opportunities across a firm's client base.

The platform is designed to work across different ledgers and AI services. Intuit said firms using Copilot, Claude, or ChatGPT will be able to connect those systems with Accountant Suite, enabling analysis of client records and recommended actions subject to approval.

For larger customers, Intuit Enterprise Suite is adding industry-specific functions. The company defines its mid-market customers as businesses with revenue from 10 million US dollars to several hundred million US dollars. Examples include consolidated views and grant-management tools for nonprofits, as well as inventory signals and industry-specific agents for manufacturers.

Intuit stock: AI platform targets accountant efficiency
sum: Intuit is broadening its artificial-intelligence strategy from software features into a unified platform for accountants, small businesses and mid-market customers. Chief Executive Sasan Goodarzi outlined the approach in remarks published by Intuit on Wednesday, November 4.

Goodarzi said Intuit is combining customer data, industry-specific workflows and artificial intelligence under the name Intuit Intelligence. The company intends to let accountants direct automated work while retaining control over decisions, with the platform serving both accounting firms and the businesses they advise.

The planned features include agentic bookkeeping and month-end close, tools for firms to build their own workflows, and automated alerts about unusual expenses or weakening profitability. Intuit also plans to match new businesses with accountants based on industry and operating needs. Some of these capabilities are available now, while others are expected over the next three to six months, according to the company.

Intuit said more than 260,000 firms use Intuit Accountant Suite. Those firms save more than nine hours per month per client, and many report spending 30% more time on advisory work rather than manual tasks. On the mid-market side, more than 25,000 businesses with revenue above 20 million US dollars use the platform and save about two days per month, the company said.

The strategy also extends to Intuit Enterprise Suite. Its tools are designed for sector-specific needs, including consolidated reporting for nonprofits and inventory signals for manufacturers. Intuit said half of the service-based businesses it serves report improved profitability after moving to Enterprise Suite.

The update gives investors a clearer view of Intuit's operating thesis: automation should increase customer engagement, improve accountant productivity and support growth in higher-value business software. The figures are management claims rather than reported financial results, so the next test will be whether usage translates into durable customer growth, retention and revenue.

sum: Intuit Inc. provides financial management, payments and capital, compliance, and marketing products and services in the United States. The company operates in two segments: Global Business Solutions and Consumer. Its Global Business Solutions segment provides QuickBooks services, which include financial and business management online services, desktop software, payroll solutions, time tracking, merchant payment processing and bill pay solutions, checking accounts, and financing services for small and mid-market businesses; and Mailchimp, a marketing automation and customer relationship management. The Consumer segment provides TurboTax, a do-it-yourself and assisted income tax preparation products and services; Credit Karma, a personal finance solution that provides recommendations for credit card, home, auto, and personal loan, and insurance products; online savings and checking accounts; and access to its credit scores and reports, credit and identity monitoring, credit report dispute, credit building tools, debt pay-down assistance, credit card rewards optimization, and connected account capabilities. This segment also offers ProTax offerings which include Lacerte, ProSeries, and ProFile desktop tax-preparation software products; and ProConnect Tax Online, electronic tax filing service, and bank products and related services. It sells products and services through direct sales channels, multichannel shop-and-buy experiences, online application stores, and partner and other channels. Intuit Inc. has a strategic collaboration with Aprio, LLP to develop AI-powered solutions designed to help identify tax planning opportunities, benchmark business performance, improve financial visibility, and support more informed decision-making across industries, including construction, dental, wealth management, and tax. Intuit Inc. was founded in 1983 and is headquartered in Mountain View, California.

sum: The back office is becoming a key battleground in financial software. Small businesses want to spend less time checking invoices, moving money and correcting mistakes, and more time running their operations. Intuit INTU and BILL Holdings BILL both aim to meet that demand through cloud platforms that combine financial data, payments and artificial intelligence. Both also benefit when customers replace disconnected spreadsheets with integrated tools and add services as their needs grow.

Their approaches, however, are different. Intuit starts with its widely used QuickBooks accounting franchise and extends into payroll, financing and mid-market management, while TurboTax and Credit Karma serve consumers. BILL concentrates on the flow of business money, helping companies manage payables, receivables, cards and expenses within one system.

Intuit brings greater scale and business diversification; BILL brings deeper specialization in payment workflows. For investors, the comparison comes down to customer engagement, execution and the ability to turn automation into sustainable earnings growth.

Intuit has established relationships with businesses, accountants and consumers, which is difficult to replicate. QuickBooks sits close to the financial records that companies use daily, making payments, payroll and lending natural extensions. Compared with BILL's more specialized approach, this broader platform offers several routes to deepen customer spending without relying on one workflow.

Its mid-market expansion is especially promising. Fiscal 2026 mid-market revenues increased 39%, supported by QuickBooks Online Advanced and Intuit Enterprise Suite. More sophisticated customers need reporting, industry-specific tools and workforce management, creating room for Intuit to serve them as their operations become more complex. Accountants also generated roughly a quarter of new Enterprise Suite contracts.

AI could strengthen these relationships. Intuit Intelligence automates tasks such as bookkeeping, cash-flow forecasting and reconciliation, while its proposed acquisition of Sequence would add automated pricing, billing and revenue recognition. These moves extend Intuit further into workflows that BILL also wants to serve, although integration and adoption remain important tests.

sum: Management now champions a new portfolio of ‘growth engines,’ but the story they quietly shelved was powered by a flagship product whose once-explosive growth has started to cool.

For Intuit (INTU) investors, the new story is loud and clear: the company is firing on all cylinders with a set of “growth engines” all expanding at a blistering pace, “north of 30%.” It’s a compelling narrative for a stock that has badly lagged the market. But the real signal for a long-term holder isn’t what’s being amplified, it’s what has gone quiet. Just over a year ago, the company’s identity was wrapped in a different, singular mission. And the silence that has settled over that old story tells you more about where the real risks and dependencies now lie.

Not long ago, you couldn’t get through an Intuit presentation without hearing about the revolution in “done-for-you experiences.” This was the core strategy. As recently as a few quarters ago, management was consistently “making progress delivering done-for-you experiences,” a concept powered by its AI assistant and embodied by its star product, TurboTax Live. The results were spectacular, with the company reporting a stunning “47% growth in TurboTax Live revenue” in that period. It was the undisputed hero of the growth story.

But listen to the latest call, and that specific drumbeat has faded. The “done-for-you” framing is largely gone, replaced by talk of “AI agents” and “autonomous execution.” While the underlying business is still there, the narrative emphasis has decisively moved on.

The new headline act is a broader, more diversified portfolio. Management now points to four key areas as the company’s future: “Assisted tax, money, portfolio and mid market, all growing north of 30%.” This is a classic and often smart strategic pivot, shifting the spotlight from one high-performing product to a basket of them. It spreads the risk and widens the story.

Here, however, is the hard number that reveals the magnitude of the shift. TurboTax Live, the former star of the “done-for-you” story, is now expected to grow revenue by 36% this year. That is still phenomenal growth. But it is a material deceleration from the 47% pace that defined the old narrative.

items.t: Intuit was an AI pioneer. Why its stock became a SaaSpocalypse casualty
sum: Does being an early adopter to AI protect a company in an AI-induced market panic?

Apparently not, based on the experience of Intuit, best known for TurboTax and QuickBooks—and the worst performing stock in the S&P 500 as this year opened. It was a twist in fate for the software company: Intuit is a big name in tax and personal accounting software, and its stock is Wall Street royalty, smashing the S&P Index over the company's 33 years as a publicly traded company. But in January and February, even as tax preparation season began, it took a drubbing in a market scare—the so-called SaaSpocalypse. Investors were suddenly gripped with the fear that AI would annihilate software companies of every kind.

For Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi, the stock's plunge was painfully ironic. Far from being caught off guard by AI, he was an early AI adopter. Years before most CEOs, he made AI a centerpiece of his company's strategy, seeing it as a powerful tool, not a competitor. He told Fortune in 2020: "In five to ten years, undisputed, it will be as powerful as the impact of electricity and the internet."

And he didn't just talk the talk: That same year, Goodarzi laid off 715 employees—unprecedented at Intuit—and hired some 700 new employees who could advance AI throughout the company. Those moves made Intuit a leading-edge business model in the AI era—a high-profile example of how to go all-in on AI and simultaneously all-in on humans. The company's example was seen by many as a portent of the AI future.

That reputation offered little protection during the SaaSpocalypse: Indeed, Intuit was the stock investors hammered most ferociously. "We got sold even more [than others] in the first six weeks of the year because we were trading so much better than our peer companies," Goodarzi says. As the stock plunged, Intuit couldn't fully respond to investors because a company quarter was closing at the end of January, so it had to observe the normal silent period.

Intuit's stock price has rebounded partially to around $350 at publication time, with a valuation of shy of $100 billion—nowhere near its 2025 year-end level and less than half its all-time high of just over $220 billion, reached last summer.
